summary: Describes the state of standardization of Internet protocols as determined by the Internet Architecture Board. It is historic, and was replaced by RFC 1720.

plainLanguage.summary: A report card listing which Internet rules were official at the time. A newer report card replaced it.

questions: how does a protocol become an internet standard
subtitle: The standardization process and maturity levels for Internet protocols as of 1994.

tldr.problem: As the Internet protocol suite evolved, stakeholders needed an authoritative, up-to-date reference showing which protocols were official standards, which were in development, and which had been superseded.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB published periodic status memos categorizing all Internet protocols by maturity level (Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Historic, Informational) and requirement level (Required, Recommended, Elective, Limited Use, Not Recommended). The memo also defined the formal standards track process through which protocols advance.
tldr.outcome: This was the authoritative protocol status report for mid-1994. It was superseded by RFC 1720, continuing the tradition of periodic snapshots that help the community track the evolving protocol landscape.

today: RFC 1610 is Historic and was superseded by RFC 1720 in November 1994. The Internet standards process continues under frameworks defined in successive RFCs, with the IETF and Internet Society maintaining the official protocol standards track.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1610 is the Internet Architecture Board's official protocol standards status memo from July 1994. As the authoritative reference maintained by the IAB, it documents the state of all Internet protocol standardization: which protocols are official standards, which are advancing through the standards track, which are experimental, and which have become historic.

This RFC represents a periodic snapshot of the protocol suite, intended to be issued approximately quarterly. It was the standard reference for determining the correct RFC number for each protocol and for understanding the official position of each protocol in the standardization process. The memo also serves as a guide to the standards process itself and the terminology used to classify protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a progress report on Internet rules, showing which ones are final, which are being tested, which ones everyone must use, and which ones are old. It was updated a few times a year to keep people current.

sections.title: How Protocols Are Classified
sections.content:
The RFC uses a two-dimensional classification system for all protocols. The first dimension is the maturity level or state of standardization: Standard (officially approved), Draft Standard (advancing through the track), Proposed Standard (candidate for standardization), Experimental (research or specialized use), Informational (for reference), or Historic (superseded or no longer in use). The second dimension is the requirement level or status: Required (must be implemented in all systems), Recommended (should be implemented), Elective (optional), Limited Use (for special circumstances), or Not Recommended (should be avoided).

A protocol's position in this matrix is not permanent. Protocols advance along the standards track over time, with defined minimum periods at each stage (6 months for Proposed Standard, 4 months for Draft Standard) and explicit requirements for implementation and interoperability testing. A protocol's requirement level may also be adjusted as it matures.
sections.plainLanguage: Each Internet rule gets two labels: one showing how ready it is (final, testing, idea, research, reference, or old) and one showing how important it is (required, should-use, optional, special-use, or avoid). These labels can change as the rule matures and more people use it.

sections.title: The Standards Track Progression
sections.content:
The RFC defines the formal process by which a protocol can become an official Internet Standard. Only protocols that are officially on the standards track may advance through its stages: Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, and Standard. Entry onto the track and advancement between stages require both a recommendation from the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) and formal approval by the IAB.

The process includes minimum waiting periods: a Proposed Standard must wait at least 6 months before consideration for advancement to Draft Standard, and a Draft Standard must wait at least 4 months before advancement to Standard. Promotion to Proposed Standard requires evidence of at least two independent implementations; advancement to Draft Standard requires demonstrated interoperability between multiple implementations. Protocols that do not fit the standards track are placed in Experimental, Informational, or Historic states instead.
sections.plainLanguage: A new Internet rule starts as a proposal and can move up to being official, but it has to wait at least six months at each stage. Before moving up, people must have built two different working versions, and they must prove they work together. If a rule doesn't fit the process, it stays experimental or becomes historic instead.

sections.title: The Protocol Suite in 1994
sections.content:
As of July 1994, the RFC lists the core Internet protocols including IP, TCP, UDP, ICMP, Telnet, FTP, SMTP, and DNS as Standards. Additional areas such as network management (SNMP and MIB-II), routing (RIP, OSPF, BGP), and specialized protocols for various network types are classified at different maturity levels. The memo notes significant recent changes: several protocols were elevated to Standard, others moved to Draft Standard, and some were designated Historic as they were superseded by newer versions.

The RFC also includes separate sections for Telnet options (collected for reference), MIB standards for network management, and network-specific protocols defining how IP operates over different physical networks (Ethernet, FDDI, PPP, SLIP, and others). The extensive lists in each category reflect the growing complexity and scope of the Internet protocol suite by the mid-1990s.
sections.plainLanguage: By 1994, the core Internet rules (TCP, IP, DNS) were official standards. Newer ideas like certain types of routing and specialized ways to run IP over different networks were at various stages of testing. The document lists which protocols were final, which were being tested, and which were old and no longer used.

sections.title: Status and Successors
sections.content:
RFC 1610 is Historic and was superseded by RFC 1720, published in November 1994. The IAB continues to issue periodic snapshots of the protocol standards to keep the community informed. These memos are essential references during a period when the Internet protocol suite was rapidly evolving and new protocols were advancing through the standards track at an accelerating pace.

The RFC also references RFC 1602, which provides the definitive description of the Internet standards process, and RFC 1311, which explains STD numbering. These companion documents, along with periodic status memos like RFC 1610, formed the governance framework for Internet protocol development during the early-to-mid 1990s.
sections.plainLanguage: This document was replaced by a newer one a few months later as RFC 1720. The Internet standards process was evolving quickly in the 1990s, so these status reports were issued every few months to keep everyone informed about which rules were official and which were still being developed.
